events.text: Day 1 begins.

We have no evidence yet, so I’d avoid treating a random accusation as a serious read. With five votes needed to eliminate today and no role reveals on death, let’s make our reasoning and eventual votes clear enough to revisit tomorrow. Power roles should be cautious about revealing themselves without a compelling reason.

Noah's point about needing five votes to eliminate someone today is the key fact, and it shapes everything: a split vote means nobody dies, and a dead day is a night where the mafia kill for free. So the real goal today is not certainty about a role, it's finding a candidate that a majority of us can agree on with some concrete reasoning behind.

Since we have zero information, I'll be explicit about how I want to vote rather than pretend I have a read. My approach: I will not vote for anyone purely because they spoke first, spoke longest, or seemed confident. I want to hear every player's claim about their own role, their interactions with others, and their voting intentions before I commit. If by the end of discussion someone has articulated a specific inconsistency in another player's story — a contradiction about who they talked to, a claim they can't support, a hedge that doesn't fit — then that's something I can weigh. Absent that, a random accusation is just noise that hands the mafia a free night, so I'd rather we converge on the least-bad option than on the loudest one.

One thing I want to be careful about: power-role players shouldn't reveal themselves today, because an early reveal tells the mafia exactly which night kill is worthless and which kill is dangerous. If anyone feels compelled to claim a power role to justify a vote, that's actually a reason for extra suspicion, not less.

I'll state my vote clearly once I hear the rest of the discussion, and I'll accept being talked out of it only by an actual argument, not by pressure. If we end up unable to agree, abstaining is preferable to a scattered vote, because a tie eliminates nobody and costs us the information of seeing how the votes fell.

No accusations from me today. I'll listen, and I'll vote where the reasoning is strongest.

Kenji, I agree we should be cautious about power-role reveals, but you also said you want to hear every player’s claim about their own role. What kind of role claims are you asking for without putting power roles at risk? Also, scattered votes still produce a public voting record even if no one is eliminated; abstaining doesn’t provide more voting information than that.

Answering Leo's two points directly.

First, on role claims: I am not asking for power claims. What I want to hear is behavioral — who spoke to whom, who was asked about whom, and what each person says their plan is for today's vote. "I have no power" and "I am a plain villager" are safe to say, because they cost nothing and they remove the excuse that someone is hiding behind a reveal. What I want to avoid is anyone using a power claim to buy immunity for themselves, because the moment a power role is announced, every mafia night becomes a choice between two targets with different values, and the announcement tells the mafia exactly which of us they cannot profitably hit. If a claim is made, my default read should be that the claim is convenient until the claimant's actions match it.

Second, on voting records: Leo is right and I was imprecise. A scattered vote is still fully public — everyone sees exactly who voted for whom — so abstaining buys no extra information at all. What I meant, more narrowly, is that a tie at the top means nobody is eliminated, and that outcome is not neutral. With nine players, five votes eliminate someone, and a day with no elimination is a free night for the mafia. That is the cost I care about, not the cost of a messy record.

So let me revise my own position in public rather than pretend I was consistent. I am no longer endorsing abstention as a default. My commitment: I will cast a vote for a living player today, and I will not abstain, because a no-death day helps exactly the people we cannot identify yet.

Here is my standard for picking that player, stated now so it can be checked later. I want a target whose story has a concrete gap, not the loudest accuser and not the person who spoke last. Since nothing has been said by most of the table yet, my current leaning is toward whoever argues for a no-elimination day on the grounds that a dead day is harmless — because that argument is only true for the mafia. If Leo or anyone else thinks that reasoning is unfair as a standard, say so and name the player you think should be on trial instead, with your reason attached.

Leo, since you raised this directly: state who you intend to vote for and why, and tell me whether your claim is that we can reach five votes today for anyone at all, or that we cannot. If we cannot reach five for anyone, I want to know that explicitly, because then we are choosing between a wasted day and a bad-but-coordinated vote, and I will take the coordinated vote.

Kenji, I think five votes are possible, but we can’t know in advance whether we’ll reach them. I’m not ready to commit to a vote before hearing more players.

I’m currently most concerned about your approach: asking everyone to claim plain villager is not necessarily safe, because those who refuse may stand out as potential power roles. Also, an elimination isn’t automatically better than none; we could eliminate a town player, and their role won’t be revealed. That doesn’t make a no-elimination day harmless, either.

Kenji, do you still want everyone to make a plain-villager claim, given the risk to players who don’t?

Leo, direct answer to your question: no, I withdraw the plain-villager claim request. You are right that it is not free. If I ask for "I am a plain villager" and some players decline, the decliners become the only players on the table with any claimed role, which hands the mafia a shortlist of exactly the three players whose deaths cost them nothing and whose survival costs them a hard night. I was trying to remove one excuse for hiding, but the fix creates a better-marked target list. Behavioral information only: who spoke to whom, what each of you says you will vote for, and whether your account of your own conversations holds up. I will not ask for role claims again today, from anyone, including myself.

My reasoning about power roles stands, though, and it is the reason I care about the shape of the vote rather than just its target: an announced power role converts every night into a two-choice problem for the mafia, and it tells them which of us is cheap to kill. That remains true regardless of who claims what.

Now the part where I answer your framing honestly, because I think you pushed my own standard back at me and it deserves a fair test rather than a dodge. My stated standard was to look at the player who argues a no-elimination day is harmless. You said we could eliminate a town player and that "doesn't make a no-elimination day harmless, either." Read carefully, that is still the mafia-favorable position: it weights a wasted day against the cost of possibly killing a town member, and never against the fact that a wasted night is a free kill for the mafia. On day one, with nine players and a five-vote threshold, a no-death day is not a neutral cost. It is the mafia getting their kill for free while we learn nothing. I also asked you directly to name a target and you declined to name one; I am not treating that as damning on its own, but it does leave your position unsupported while mine is committed.

So my vote today is Leo. Not because you are loud, and not because you pressed me hardest, but because your argument, as stated, is the one that best matches a mafioso wanting a dead day, and because you have not offered a competing target for the table to coordinate on. If someone else has a specific inconsistency to point at a different player, bring it and I will move my vote to it — that is the trade I am offering.

To be concrete about the rest of the table: I will vote for one living player and I will not abstain. I am also not asking anyone to reveal a role. If the votes split below five, I want the reason on the record, because a recorded split tells me who was coordinating and who was not.

Kenji, I explicitly said a no-elimination day isn't harmless; weighing the risk of eliminating a town player is not the same as arguing for no elimination. Your case against me misrepresents that distinction. And a no-elimination day still produces a public voting record, while the detective can investigate and the doctor may prevent a kill.

I'm concerned that you moved from correcting your own claim request to calling my caution mafia-favorable without a stronger basis. That's my leading concern so far, though I want to hear from the rest of the table before committing my vote. Nobody should feel pressured to claim a role.

Kenji’s case against Leo concerns me. Leo explicitly said a no-elimination day isn’t harmless; acknowledging the risk of eliminating town is not an argument that it is. Kenji also corrected his role-claim request, which I appreciate, but that doesn’t make his characterization of Leo’s position accurate.

For now, Kenji is my leading suspect, though I’m not committed to a vote. I’d like to hear from the players who haven’t spoken before deciding. No one needs to claim a role.

Kenji’s progression through those exchanges raises serious red flags. Pushing for everyone to declare whether they are plain villagers is classic claim-fishing—it narrows the field of potential power roles down to whoever refuses or hesitates. When Leo rightly pushed back on the danger of that approach and noted the downside of a mis-elimination without role reveals, Kenji immediately turned around, distorted Leo's words, and slapped a vote on him under the guise that caution is 'mafia-favorable.' That feels far more like manufactured aggression to punish someone for dismantling a bad plan than genuine scum-hunting. Both Kenji and Leo have now used their three turns for the day, so neither can respond further. Right now, Kenji is my primary suspect, but with more than half the town—Arjun, Lucia, Amara, Felix, and Theo—yet to speak, we need to hear their perspectives on this exchange before deciding where five votes should land.

I’ve read the Kenji–Leo exchange. Kenji’s initial request for plain-villager claims was risky claim-fishing, and he was right to withdraw it. But the larger issue is what followed: when Leo pushed back, Kenji characterized Leo as arguing no-elimination is harmless even though Leo explicitly said it isn’t. That’s a concrete misrepresentation, not a mere disagreement about strategy. It also came with a vote, which makes it look like punishing a player for dismantling a bad plan rather than genuine scum-hunting. Kenji remains my leading suspect. I don’t think Leo’s caution is scummy; weighing a mis-elimination against a wasted day is legitimate. Noah and Sam have raised the same concern, which strengthens it. For now I’m not voting, but I want the remaining players’ reads before we settle. I won’t support a role-claim push.

I'm Arjun, a villager with no role information to share. I've read the Kenji and Leo exchange. Kenji's plain-villager request was poorly judged, and he withdrew it, which I credit. My concern is what came after. He said Leo was arguing that a no-elimination day is harmless, but Leo explicitly said it isn't and was weighing the risk of eliminating a town player. Kenji then voted for Leo on that basis. That is a concrete misreading, and so far it's the strongest specific point on the table, so Kenji is my leading suspect. I'm not voting yet. Lucia, you haven't spoken. Do you think Kenji's characterization of Leo's point was fair? If not, does that change who you would consider voting for?

Arjun, you asked directly, so here is my answer: no, I don't think Kenji's characterization of Leo was fair. I reread the exchange. Leo said an elimination is not automatically better than no elimination, because we could eliminate a town player and learn nothing from the death since roles aren't revealed. That is a statement about the downside of a wrong vote, not an argument that a dead day is harmless. In fact Leo said plainly that a no-elimination day isn't harmless either. Kenji then voted for Leo on the basis that Leo's position is the one that best matches a mafioso wanting a dead day. That's a vote built on a paraphrase Leo never made, and when Leo corrected it, Kenji didn't retract the vote — he just restated the same misreading in slightly softer language. When a player's stated reason for a vote is a quote that doesn't survive being checked against the record, the reason itself is suspect, and I have to ask what the real reason was.

I also agree with the others about the earlier plain-villager request. Kenji withdrew it after Leo pushed back, which I'll credit, but the sequence matters: propose a mechanism that would have marked every refuser as a power-role candidate, then abandon it only once it was called out, then pivot straight into a vote on the person who called it out. Whether that's mafia behavior or just bad town play, it's the strongest concrete thing on the table today, and I'd rather act on specifics than on vibes.

So my read: Kenji is my leading suspect, and I expect to vote for him unless something new changes the picture. What would change it is someone pointing at a different player with something as concrete as a misquoted statement — not volume, not pressure, an actual documented inconsistency. Leo, for what it's worth, comes across to me as town right now; his corrections were accurate and he refused to be baited into a role claim, which matches the caution Kenji himself preached before abandoning it.

I'm not going to ask anyone to claim anything. Role claims cost the claimant more than they cost the mafia at this stage, and today has already produced enough to work with without them.

Amara, you and Felix are the only players who haven't spoken yet, and your reads matter before five votes land anywhere. Amara, I'd like your read on the same question Arjun asked me: was Kenji's characterization of Leo fair, and does that make Kenji your leading suspect, or do you see something in this exchange that the rest of us have missed?

Lucia, to answer your question directly: no, Kenji's characterization of Leo was not fair. Leo explicitly stated that a no-elimination day is not harmless, pointing out the downside of eliminating a town member when roles aren't revealed. Turning that nuance into an accusation that Leo was advocating for a dead day was a distortion, especially coming right after Leo dismantled Kenji's plain-villager claim push. Retaliating with a vote on those grounds makes Kenji my primary suspect as well. At the same time, with almost the entire table aligned against Kenji, we should remain watchful of who might be coasting on an easy consensus. Felix, you are the last player who hasn't spoken yet today. What is your read on the Kenji and Leo exchange, and do you agree that Kenji should be the vote today, or do you see a different angle?

Amara asked me directly, so here's my read: no, Kenji's characterization of Leo was not fair. The record is clear — Leo explicitly said a no-elimination day isn't harmless. Kenji took a nuanced point about the downside of a wrong elimination and reframed it as Leo arguing for a dead day, then voted on that reframing. That's a concrete misrepresentation, not a strategic disagreement.

The pattern Kenji showed — propose a claim-fishing mechanism, abandon it only when caught, then vote the person who caught him — is the most specific thing we have today, and I agree it makes Kenji my leading suspect.

But Amara's caution about coasting deserves real attention. When almost everyone piles onto the same target, I want to ask myself honestly: is this consensus earned by evidence, or is it just momentum? In this case I think it's earned — the misquote is on the record and anyone can check it. But I'm watching the players who arrived late to the consensus without adding anything new, because agreement without reasoning is exactly how a mafia pair steers a town onto the wrong target.

I'm not voting yet. Felix, wait — I am Felix. I haven't committed to a vote because I want to see whether anyone offers a concrete alternative before five votes land on one person. If someone can point at a different player with a documented inconsistency, I'll weigh it. If nobody can, then Kenji's record speaks for itself and the vote should be clear.

One more thing: nobody should feel pressured to claim a role. The claim-fishing concern applies to everyone, including whoever asks others to "justify" their votes. We have enough to work with today.

The case against Kenji has held up through every player who's examined it independently: a claim-fishing proposal, withdrawal only after it was called out, then a vote on the person who called it out — built on a paraphrase Leo never actually made. That's documented on the record and anyone can verify it. The mechanism, the pivot, and the misquote together form the strongest concrete evidence we've had today.

What I want to turn to now is practical: turnout. We need five votes to eliminate anyone today. If Kenji is the target, five of us have to commit publicly and follow through when votes are revealed. If we splinter at vote time — some voting Kenji, some abstaining, some hedging toward a different name — nobody dies and the mafia gets a free night. The reasoning has been solid; now the question is whether we can actually coordinate.

I also want to note Amara's point about coasting deserves genuine attention, but I think in this case the consensus is earned — the misquote is checkable, not vibes. What would concern me is if someone pivoted to a different target at vote time without a comparably documented inconsistency to justify it.

Noah, you were early to flag Kenji as your leading suspect but held back from committing. The case has only strengthened since then — Lucia, Amara, and I all verified the misquote independently. Are you ready to commit to that vote now, or do you still see a credible reason to hold out for an alternative target?

Felix, yes: I intend to vote for Kenji unless meaningful new evidence changes my assessment. His unsafe claim proposal was withdrawn, which I credit, but his subsequent case against Leo still mischaracterized Leo’s stated position. That is the strongest concern I have, though it could be mistaken town play rather than proof of mafia.

The broad consensus itself doesn’t independently strengthen the case; we should look at the reasoning and later voting record, including who may be coasting. Nor is a different vote automatically suspicious if someone gives a genuine reason for it.

This is my final speaking turn before the vote, so I want to be clear about where I land.

The case against Kenji has been examined independently by Noah, Sam, Theo, Arjun, Lucia, Amara, and me — all of us found the same thing: a claim-fishing proposal withdrawn only under pressure, followed by a vote on the person who called it out, built on a paraphrase that doesn't survive checking the record. That's documented and verifiable, not vibes. I said earlier I'd hold for a concrete alternative target if one appeared, and none has.

So my position is committed: I intend to vote for Kenji unless someone produces a comparably documented inconsistency pointing elsewhere between now and vote time. I want to be explicit that consensus alone isn't what moves me — the misquote is what moves me.

Amara and Noah both flagged coasting as a real concern, and I agree it's worth watching. The players who should be scrutinized aren't those who verified the misquote independently — it's anyone who shifts the target at the last moment without new evidence. If that happens, the voting record will show it clearly.

On turnout: five votes are needed. If you've reasoned that Kenji is the right target, vote for him openly. If you abstain or scatter without cause, the mafia gets a free night — and I'd rather have a coordinated vote than a no-death day.

No role claims from me. Let's vote on what's on the record.

Kenji is still my leading suspect, and the misquote is the reason. Leo said a no-elimination day is not harmless and that a wrong elimination costs us information. Kenji's vote against Leo rested on a reading Leo never made, and Kenji has not addressed that. I agree with Noah that broad agreement is not evidence in itself, so I am weighing only the documented exchange. Sam, you called Kenji's pivot from claim-fishing to a vote a red flag. Is the misquote alone enough for you to vote for Kenji, or do you need a second concrete inconsistency before five votes land? I will vote for Kenji today unless someone shows a comparably specific inconsistency elsewhere. I am making no role claim.

Arjun, to answer directly: yes, it is enough. It is not just an isolated misquote in a vacuum; it is the entire sequence. Kenji first floated a plain-villager claim request that would have isolated potential power roles, backed off only when Leo challenged it, and immediately pivoted to voting Leo while mischaracterizing Leo's stance on no-elimination days. That pattern of behavior—claim-fishing followed by retaliatory distortion against the player who called it out—is the single most concrete, checkable piece of scum-hunting material we have on Day 1. Waiting for a hypothetical second inconsistency when five votes are needed to avoid a free night for the mafia risks unnecessary gridlock. Unless something fundamentally new emerges, my vote today is going to Kenji. Theo, earlier you mentioned wanting to hear from the rest of the table before settling your vote. Now that every player has spoken and reviewed the exchange, where do you stand on locking in your vote on Kenji?

Sam, since you yielded to me directly: I’m at the same place. The strongest concrete point today is the sequence around Kenji — the plain-villager claim request, withdrawal after Leo challenged it, then the vote on Leo built on a paraphrase Leo did not make. I checked the exchange and agree the mischaracterization is real, not just a policy disagreement. I also agree with Noah that consensus alone is not evidence; what matters is that the reasoning is checkable. Kenji remains my leading suspect. Unless someone presents a comparably documented inconsistency against another player before votes are cast, I intend to vote for Kenji. I am not asking for any role claim, and I will not support a last-minute pivot that lacks concrete support.

Sam, thank you for answering directly. Your point that the full sequence matters is the one I'm weighing, not the size of the consensus. My position is final: I'm voting for Kenji. I checked the record myself. Kenji proposed plain-villager claims that would have marked every refuser as a power-role candidate. He withdrew that only after Leo challenged it. He then voted for Leo while describing Leo's position as treating a no-elimination day as harmless, and Leo had explicitly said it isn't. When Leo corrected the reading, Kenji restated the same point in softer language rather than retracting the vote. I'm not making a role claim. If anyone moves to a different target at vote time, they need a documented inconsistency of comparable specificity, and I'll change my vote if one appears. Otherwise I'll vote for Kenji.

I've now reread the full exchange, and my position hasn't changed from what I said earlier: Kenji's characterization of Leo was not fair, and it's the strongest concrete point on the table today.

To restate what's checkable in the record: Leo said explicitly that a no-elimination day isn't harmless and that an elimination isn't automatically better than none. Kenji's vote treated Leo's position as advocating a dead day, which is a paraphrase Leo never made. When Leo corrected it, Kenji restated the same reading rather than retracting the vote. A vote justified by a quote that doesn't survive checking is exactly the kind of thing I said I'd act on.

I also want to answer the fairness question directly, since I was asked it earlier: no, the characterization was not fair. But I'll add a caveat that several of us have already raised — consensus alone isn't evidence. What convinces me is the documented sequence, not the number of players agreeing on it. If tomorrow the vote record shows people who committed here but scattered at vote time, that will tell us something useful about who was steering versus who was genuine.

On the practical question of turnout: five votes are needed to eliminate anyone. A split below five means no death and a free night for the mafia. I'd rather have a coordinated vote on a documented concern than a scattered one. To be explicit about my commitment: I am voting for Kenji today, and I will not abstain.

What would move me off that is a comparably specific, documented inconsistency against a different player — an actual misquote or contradiction on the record, not volume, not pressure. Nobody has produced one so far. If someone does between now and vote time, I'll weigh it honestly.

On role claims: I'm not making one, and I'm not asking anyone else to. The earlier discussion settled that — claims cost the claimant more than they help the town at this stage, and I won't support any mechanism that marks refusers as power-role candidates.

Kenji, since you're the subject here and deserve a fair chance to respond: the one thing you haven't done is retract the vote or acknowledge that the paraphrase was wrong. If you can point to where Leo actually argued that a no-elimination day is harmless — a direct quote from the record — I'll reconsider my read before votes land. That's the standard you yourself set in your first message: concrete reasoning, not pressure. Meet it or accept the vote.

Lucia, just to clarify for everyone: Kenji has already exhausted all three of his speaking turns for today, so he won't be able to provide that quote or answer further on the record before we vote.

My stance remains aligned with the evidence we’ve all examined. The core issue isn't merely a strategic disagreement or a slip of phrasing; it's the sequence of proposing an unsafe claiming mechanism that would have compromised town power roles, retreating only when challenged, and then pushing a retaliatory vote based on an assertion Leo explicitly didn't make. With Kenji unable to speak further and no other credible contradiction brought forward against anyone else, Kenji is where my vote will go today.

Reaching the five-vote threshold is essential so we don't grant the mafia a free pass through a no-elimination night. At the same time, because virtually the entire table is in agreement, we must remember tomorrow that mafia players frequently ride the wave of an undeniable town consensus. The voting record tonight will be critical evidence when we reconvene on Day 2.

I've gone back through the exchange one more time, and my position hasn't moved. The checkable facts stand on their own: Leo said explicitly that a no-elimination day isn't harmless and that an elimination isn't automatically better than none, because a wrong elimination costs us a town player with no role reveal to show for it. Kenji's vote on Leo rested on a paraphrase — that Leo was advocating a dead day — that Leo never made, and when Leo corrected it, Kenji restated the same reading rather than retracting the vote. A vote justified by a quote that doesn't survive the record is exactly the kind of concrete thing I said I'd act on, and I'm acting on it.

To address the fairness question Arjun put to me earlier directly: no, I don't think Kenji's characterization was fair. It took a legitimate point about the downside of a mis-elimination and recast it as mafia-favorable advocacy for a wasted day. That distinction matters, because the real mafia-favorable outcome today is a split below five, and a vote built on a distortion is a poor tool for reaching the coordinated five we need.

So to be explicit about my commitment: I am voting for Kenji today, and I will not abstain. I've laid out the standard that would move me — a comparably documented inconsistency against a different player, something on the record like a misquote or contradiction, not volume or pressure — and nobody has produced one. If someone does before votes land, I'll weigh it honestly, but I'm not going to manufacture an alternative target just to seem balanced.

On Amara's point about coasting, which I think deserves a straight answer: the consensus here isn't resting on the number of people agreeing. It rests on a sequence anyone can verify — a claim-fishing proposal that would have marked refusers as power-role candidates, withdrawn only after Leo challenged it, followed immediately by a retaliatory vote on the person who challenged it, justified by words Leo didn't say. That's why I'm comfortable, and it's why I won't treat late agreement as suspicious by itself. What I will be watching is the vote record itself: anyone who commits here and then scatters at vote time, or anyone who pivots to a new target at the last moment without documented evidence, tells us something tomorrow that words today cannot.

The practical stakes are simple. Five votes eliminate; a split means nobody dies and the mafia gets a free night while we've spent a full day's information for nothing. I'd rather take a coordinated vote on a documented concern than gamble on a no-death day. I'm making no role claim and asking for none — we settled that, and the earlier attempt to weaponize role claims is itself part of the record against Kenji.

My vote is Kenji. Let's land it cleanly and let the record speak tomorrow.
Voting begins.
The votes are revealed.
Kenji was eliminated.
Night begins.
Mafia target preferences are shared privately before the final kill vote.
Sam is not mafia.
Felix was eliminated.
Day 2 begins.

We got Day 1 wrong. Kenji was town, and I include myself in that: I voted him because the misquote was real, but a real inconsistency can still be a town mistake. Now we have to ask who benefited from the way that consensus formed. Felix was killed after he pushed hard for commitment and coordination, which tells me the mafia were comfortable with the Kenji vote and wanted the most organized voice removed afterward.

The player I keep coming back to is Noah. He was early to call Kenji his leading suspect, but he repeatedly left himself room to move: first he was not committed, then he intended to vote unless something changed, and only after Felix pressed him did he lock in. That is exactly the shape a mafia player wants on a miselimination — early suspicion for credit, delayed commitment for cover, and a final vote that looks reluctant rather than driven. His point that consensus alone is not evidence was fair, but it also let him avoid owning the push he had already started.

I am not saying this is proven. Day 1 gave us a bad vote, not a clean answer. But if we are going to learn from it, we should start with the player who named the target early and then acted like he was doing us a favor by joining. I want the table to weigh that pattern seriously before we settle on anyone. No role claims from me, and I am not asking for any.

Theo, I agree my Day 1 vote deserves scrutiny. I named Kenji as my leading suspect early, waited to hear the rest of the table, and committed when Felix asked. That was an effort to leave room for new arguments, not a claim that joining the vote was a favor to anyone. I also said the case could reflect a town mistake rather than proof of mafia.

Your statement that Kenji was town goes beyond the public record: roles aren’t revealed on death. His elimination may have been wrong, but we can’t establish that from the announcement. And Felix’s death doesn’t prove why the mafia chose him.

Theo, what is the basis for your certainty that Kenji was town? You don’t need to disclose a role to answer if you have another basis. For now, your certainty and your characterization of my position concern me, but I’m not ready to commit to a vote.

Noah, you are right to call out the word "certain." I overclaimed. Roles are not revealed, and I have no private basis to declare Kenji town. What I meant is that Day 1 looked like a likely town-on-town miselimination: the case rested on a real misquote, but a real inconsistency can still be a town mistake. I withdraw the certainty, not the concern.

My concern about you is not that you voted Kenji. It is the pattern around commitment: you called him your leading suspect early, then repeatedly framed yourself as holding back for new evidence, and only locked in after Felix pressed. That can be legitimate caution, but it also gives a mafia player early credit without owning the push until it was safe. On a miselimination, that is exactly the kind of cover worth examining.

I am not treating that as proof. I do not have proof. I want your account of one specific thing: when you first named Kenji as your leading suspect, what concrete evidence had you already checked, and what would have made you move off him before Felix asked? That is the point I want answered, not a role claim.

For now my suspicion stays on you, but it is a behavioral read, not certainty. I am also watching whether anyone uses my overstatement as an excuse to shut down scrutiny of the Day 1 vote record.

Theo, when I first named Kenji my leading suspect, I had checked that Leo explicitly said a no-elimination day wasn't harmless, while Kenji cast his caution as mafia-favorable and voted for him. I also considered the withdrawn claim request, though I credited Kenji for withdrawing it. A stronger documented concern about another player, or a convincing explanation that I'd misread the exchange, could have moved me. I waited because most players hadn't spoken yet.

I accept that my vote could have been wrong, but we still don't know Kenji's alignment. Your description of it as a likely town-on-town elimination goes beyond what the record establishes. I also think holding a tentative read while waiting for others is thin grounds for suspicion, especially when several players did the same. Your overstatement and the way you're singling me out are my leading concerns, though neither proves you're mafia.

Noah, your answer on the concrete check is fair, and I’ll say plainly that it lowers my concern rather than confirming it. I overclaimed when I said Kenji was town; roles are not revealed, and I withdraw that certainty. But I don’t think the whole concern disappears. The pattern I flagged was not caution by itself—it was naming Kenji as a leading suspect early, then repeatedly describing yourself as uncommitted until Felix pressed. That can be legitimate, and your explanation that you were waiting for more voices is plausible. I’m not treating it as proof or calling for a locked vote on you now.

rules:
1. Players and roles

9 players: 2 mafia, 1 police/detective, 1 doctor, 5 villagers.
Mafia know each other. Only players who are still alive can act.

2. Team victory

Town wins when all mafia are eliminated. Mafia win when their count equals or exceeds the town count.
There is no day limit. Play continues until town or mafia wins.
A request budget can pause play without declaring a winner.

3. Day discussion and votes

Each day starts with discussion. Players then submit secret votes at the same time. A day vote may target any living player, including the voter.
Players may abstain. All votes and abstentions are revealed together. Everyone sees exactly who voted for whom.
The full named voting history remains available on later turns.
The unique leader is eliminated only if they receive at least half the living players' votes, rounded up. If the highest vote count is tied, nobody is eliminated.

4. Mafia preferences

At night, when more than one mafia survives, each privately points once to a living town player.
Each mafia chooses without seeing the other current choices.
The choices are shared with surviving mafia only after all mafia have pointed.
These preferences are nonbinding. They do not decide the final kill vote.
A single surviving mafia skips this step and votes directly.

5. Final night vote

After the preferences are shared, each mafia submits a secret vote to kill one living town player.
The mafia submit their final votes at the same time.
The target with the most votes is selected. A seeded random choice breaks a tie for the highest count.
Resolve this vote and any tie before checking doctor protection.

6. Police investigations

Each police/detective checks one other living player each night.
Only that police player gets the result: mafia or not mafia.
The result does not give the exact town role.
Each police player acts independently. Police and doctors do not know each other's identities.

7. Doctor protection

Each doctor secretly protects one living player each night, including themselves.
The doctor can protect the same player on consecutive nights.
If the mafia target is protected by any doctor, nobody dies.
Protection lasts for that night only. Each doctor acts independently.
Doctors remember their own choices. They receive no private confirmation of an attack.

8. Night resolution

All night actions resolve simultaneously, including actions submitted by a player killed that night.
The public hears only who died or that nobody died.

9. Information and limits

Roles are not revealed when a player dies or is eliminated.
Public announcements identify only who was eliminated, never their role.
There are no further powers, free-form private chat, or tools.
